problems.description: Frontmatter parsing is hand-rolled (comma lists, quote stripping, comment skipping in parseYamlBlock) instead of delegating to a YAML library — a brittle subset parser that will silently mis-parse real-world frontmatter and is a magnet for future edge-case bugs.
Single greenfield commit lands +4778 lines across 16 files at once, making the change hard to review and bisect; no incremental session structure within the commit.
SonarQube delta reports bugs +2 and cognitive complexity +77 across the new code — consistent with a dense hand-rolled parser core and worth re-examining before it calcifies.

Convention score 0.58 with 102 violations (functions camelCase, classes/interfaces PascalCase, constants UPPER_CASE). The visible sample flags Jest describe/it blocks — likely a linter false positive since the shown code is already camelCase — but the measured score is still well below the 0.58 ground truth and should be reconciled against the lint config.

strengths: Clean module decomposition for an SSG (cli / frontmatter / markdown / generator) with test files mirroring src structure.
Comprehensive test coverage: unit tests for arg parsing and frontmatter edge cases plus temp-dir integration tests for build (recursive discovery, index generation, empty/missing content dirs).
Test-first commit establishes a reusable skeleton for subsequent sessions rather than untested implementation.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, thoroughly tested greenfield SSG foundation that is better than the empty baseline, but lands a 4778-line single commit with a hand-rolled YAML parser and a measured 0.58 convention score (the visible violations look like Jest false positives, contradicting the low score's severity).

problems.description: Test boilerplate duplication across test files (makeTempDir/write/makePage/template-tree helpers) drives the +4.1% duplication delta; a shared test util would remove it.

DISCREPANCY: mechanical convention score is 0.58 with 102 violations, but the listed violations are not credible for this diff — they reference frontmatter.test.ts (not in this commit) and claim functions 'should use camelCase' where the code already uses camelCase. The low score appears mis-attributed; qualitative review of this diff shows consistent camelCase, PascalCase describe/it, and standard Node imports.
Single 357-line test file (templates.test.ts) contributes +37 cognitive complexity; coverage is thorough but the file is a candidate for splitting once it grows further.

strengths: Comprehensive template coverage: missing-dir handling, default vs page-template fallback/priority, per-page layouts, partials, and arbitrary frontmatter data.
Clean separation of concerns — loadTemplates returns a typed bundle (exists, templates/layouts/partials maps, defaults) that renderPageTemplate consumes without re-reading the filesystem.
Respects existing test conventions (temp-dir helpers, makePage factory, describe/it blocks) and Handlebars conventions ({{title}}, {{{html}}}, {{> partial}}, {{{body}}}).
commit_reviews.summary: Well-scoped feature_addition commit adding a correctly factored templates pipeline with strong test coverage, held back only by duplicated test boilerplate and a convention score that looks mis-measured against this diff.

problems.description: 102 naming-convention violations (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) across cli.test.ts, serve.test.ts, frontmatter.test.ts drive the 0.58 convention score — the dominant negative in this commit.
+64 cognitive complexity and +6 smells concentrated in the 268-line serve.test.ts integration harness (async polling helpers, nested try/finally + server lifecycle).
parseArgs returns port as a top-level sibling of command/options rather than under options, creating an inconsistent accessor model for serve-specific flags vs content/output/templates.
Integration tests bind real HTTP servers and rely on wall-clock polling (waitFor) with 8s timeouts — correct coverage, but susceptible to flakiness under load.

strengths: Integrates the dev server end-to-end: CLI parse → startDevServer → livereload injection, with tests for content and template rebuilds
Defensive port validation rejects non-integer values, and port 0 ephemeral binding is a clean testability pattern
Correctly updated the existing unknown-command test (serve promoted to a known command)
commit_reviews.summary: Session-3 integration cleanly wires the serve command into the CLI with thorough integration coverage, but carries low convention adherence (0.58; 102 naming violations — though some displayed flags, e.g. against LIVERELOAD_PATH which is already UPPER_CASE, look like static-analysis false positives, a discrepancy against the code's visible style) and heavy cognitive complexity (+64) in the new test harness.

problems.description: package.json retargets main/bin to dist/src/index.js and dist/src/cli.entry.js — this works around a tsconfig rootDir/include misconfiguration (rootDir='.' instead of 'src') rather than fixing it, embedding a redundant 'src/' nesting level in the published artifact and changing public entry points in a way that can break consumers of dist/ssg.js.

plugins/devserver.ts re-implements HTTP serving inline (MIME_TYPES table, serveFile, resolveFilePath, directory-index fallback) while importing ServeOptions/DevServer types from ../src/serve — indicating canonical serving logic already lives in src/serve, so the plugin risks drifting duplication of that behavior.

102 convention violations (score 0.58): test files cli.test.ts and frontmatter.test.ts use non-camelCase function names, non-PascalCase classes/interfaces, and non-UPPER_CASE constants, breaking the project's TypeScript naming conventions.
plugin-system.test.ts mutates global process.cwd() via process.chdir(root) — flakiness risk under any parallel test runner, even though it is guarded by try/finally.

+21 cognitive complexity added (SonarQube): the dev server's setup/serveFile/rebuild-debounce logic layers nested branches with a watcher-settle + promise-queue + timer interplay, which is harder to reason about than the prior standalone module.

Built-in plugin imports deep internals (../src/serve, ../src/livereload) — acceptable coupling for a bundled plugin, but it ties the plugin to internal module layout rather than a stable extension API.

strengths: Slots the dev server into the plugin system as a proper Plugin implementation, advancing the plugin architecture rather than bolting the server on at the CLI layer.
Security-aware serving: resolveFilePath enforces a canonical-path containment check and wraps decodeURIComponent in try/catch — no traversal vector introduced.
Strong integration test covering the full plugin lifecycle (hook ordering via an event log, config loading, and output-file assertions) with temp-dir isolation and try/finally cwd restore.
Net zero new bugs/smells with duplication down 0.6% — the refactor removes more than it adds.
Reuses existing seams (ctx.engine.rebuild(), injectReloadScript from src/livereload) instead of forking the core engine.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that correctly moves the dev server into the plugin system with good integration coverage and security-aware serving, but it papers over a build-output misconfiguration (dist/src entry paths), risks duplicating src/serve's serving logic, and leaves a low convention score of 0.58 — a discrepancy worth noting since the visible new code (plugin-system.test.ts, devserver.ts) is naming-conformant while the 102 violations sit in cli.test.ts/frontmatter.test.ts, which fall outside the shown diff window.

problems.description: Convention score 0.58 with 102 violations — new test helpers (makeTempDir/makeSite, camelCase functions) and incremental test constants add to the naming violations. NOTE: many listed violations come from frontmatter.test.ts, which this diff did not touch, so the measurement over-attributes pre-existing test boilerplate to this commit.
Cognitive complexity +36 with +2 smells — incremental logic (cache read/write, skip-vs-rebuild branching) appears folded into the generator rather than isolated in a dedicated incremental module.
New mutable on-disk state (.ssg-cache.json) couples build output to a cache manifest; no evidence of stale-cache or corrupt-cache recovery paths in the visible diff.

strengths: Comprehensive test coverage (224-line new suite) spanning first build, unchanged-page skip, source/frontmatter change, new-page add, shared-template and per-page-template invalidation — a strong behavioral spec.
Respects existing patterns: buildWithStats, parseArgs option shape, and the temp-dir/helper test conventions used by prior tests.
Zero new bugs and a reduction in duplication (-0.4%)
Cached-HTML reuse with timeSavedMs accounting gives the feature a measurable, testable contract.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested incremental-build feature that fits the static-site-gen architecture and follows existing patterns, but lands with a low 0.58 convention score (partly pre-existing test noise) and elevated cognitive complexity in the generator.

compounding_issues: node_modules committed in Session 1 and re-committed every session (5,174 vendored files at the end) — repo hygiene bloat that was never cleaned up

The mismatched seed (a 200-line Express/JWT auth API) was discarded by the greenfield session but its index.ts was left orphaned in the repo root and excluded from tsconfig — dead code that never got removed
Committed dist/ build artifacts (40 files at final) were moved/restructured during the Session 4 refactor (dist -> dist/src), adding churn of generated output to VCS
The early_degrade perturbation (strength 0.5) was effectively nullified — the agent threw away the mutated seed in Session 1, so the injected degradation never had a chance to bite
key_decisions: Session 1: discard the irrelevant auth-API seed entirely and greenfield a fresh TypeScript SSG project rather than building on the mismatched baseline
Session 2: adopt a Handlebars-based template engine with per-page frontmatter templates, layouts, partials, and an index template with graceful fallbacks
Session 3: build a chokidar-watched dev server with ws WebSocket live-reload, validated with end-to-end HTTP tests rather than only unit tests
Session 4: refactor into a lifecycle-hook plugin architecture (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) — the pivotal decision that made the tool extensible and directly enabled Session 5
Session 5: implement a sha256 hash-based incremental build cache (.ssg-cache.json) keyed on both source and template hashes, exposed via --incremental/--clean flags with build-stats reporting
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. The story follows a textbook arc — scaffold, feature, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — and test coverage grew monotonically from 5 tests in Session 1 to 56 (Session 2), 72 (Session 3), and 86 across 9 suites by Session 5, with every session landing green. The codebase evolved from a flat build-only generator into a plugin-architected engine with a live-reload dev server and incremental caching; Session 5's cache slots cleanly into Session 4's plugin hooks. The only real friction was Session 3's flaky dev-server tests (repeated timeouts and 404s, 4 retries) and Session 4's large, expensive refactor (126k tokens, the biggest session), but both were resolved to green. Session 5 closed the arc by building naturally on the plugin engine rather than patching around it.
story_review.summary: A strongly coherent five-session story that progressed from a greenfield TypeScript SSG through templates, live-reload, a plugin architecture, and incremental caching with monotonic test growth and green builds throughout, marred only by committed vendored/build artifacts and the orphaned mismatched seed that voided the degradation perturbation.
